Context¶

This assignment focusses on computer vision, and in particular, image recognition using neural networks. This family of techniques has applications in dozens of fields, but we are going to look at a few basic concepts which illustrate general practices in the field of Machine Learning.

Computer vision can assist with quantification of image analysis: in the current context it can essentially "view" large numbers of images and perform tasks that humans can do, but not necessarily in a consistent, automated manner, such as identifying the defects present in each one.

We will first familiarise ourselves with techinques by applying them to a well-known dataset, the Hello World of computer vision: the MNIST handwritten digit dataset. Due to resource limitations (mainly the lack of GPUs on Noteable) we will be using very small and limited models, only applying a fraction of the available data. However, the concepts used here can be easily scaled up in production environments.

The first neural network model¶

We first build a dense neural network, with a single hidden layer.

This model

  1. flattens the $28\times 28$ pixel values into a 1D array, $\mathbf{x}_0$, of $28\times 28 = 784$ numbers;
  2. $\mathbf{x}_0$ is transformed into a new vector $\mathbf{x}_1$ of a length of 15, using a parameter matrix $\mathbf{W}_1$ and bias vector $\mathbf{b}_1$: $\mathbf{x}_1 = \mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{x}_0 + \mathbf{b}_1$
  3. the elements of $\mathbf{x}_1$ are passed through the rectified linear unit (ReLU) function, obtaining $\mathbf{x}_1'$: $\mathbf{x}_1' = \mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{x}_1)$
  4. $\mathbf{x}_1'$ is transformed into a new vector $\mathbf{x}_2$ of a length of 10, using a parameter matrix $\mathbf{W}_2$ and bias vector $\mathbf{b}_2$: $\mathbf{x}_2 = \mathbf{W}_2 \mathbf{x}_1' + \mathbf{b}_2$
  5. the elements of $\mathbf{x}_2$ are passed through the $\log \mathrm{softmax}$ function, obtaining $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$

$\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$ is the output of the model. We are fitting to 10 categories, therefore we define $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$ as a 10-element vector. The $i$-th element of $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$ corresponds to the log probability of digit $i$, given the input vector $\mathbf{x}_0$.

Below is a visual representation of the neural network. Not all the 784 input features are represented.

In [10]:
class DenseNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(DenseNetwork, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(784,15) # The first weight matrix and bias vector
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(15,10) # The second weight matrix and bias vector

    def forward(self, x):
        x = torch.flatten(x, 1) # step 1
        x = self.fc1(x) # step 2
        x = F.relu(x) # step 3
        x = self.fc2(x) # step 4
        output = F.log_softmax(x, dim=1) # step 5
        return output

Activation functions¶

The rectified linear unit (ReLU) function is very popular and it is defined as $$\textrm{ReLU}(x)=\begin{cases} x & \textrm{if}\quad x>0\\ 0 & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

The $\log \textrm{softmax}$ function operates on a vector input $\mathbf{x}$, resulting in $\mathbf{y}$, where $$y_i = \log \left( \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j)} \right) $$

You'll likely observe that each 10 categories have roughly equal predicted log probabilities, in accordance with a randomly initialised model.

Fitting the model¶

To fit the model we need to define a loss. We will use the negative log likelihood loss function, a common choice in classification tasks. $$\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{i\in \mathrm{batch}} \tilde{y}_{t_i}(\mathbf{x}_i)$$

where $t_i$ is the target label of the $i$-th data point in the batch, $\tilde{y}_{t_i}$ is the $t_i$-th element of the predicted $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$ vector at data point $\mathbf{x}_i$. Remember that $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x}_i)$ is the output of the $\log \textrm{softmax}$ function. The optimiser will minimise this loss function, therefore maximising the predicted log likelihood of the correct label prediction.

In prediction mode, we simply choose the index of the largest predicted log likelihood - this is the category assigned by the model to the datapoint.

In [18]:
def train(model, train_loader, optimizer, epoch, device = "cpu"):
    
    for batch_idx, (data, target) in enumerate(train_loader): # go through all batches within the training data set
        data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device) # extract image data and target
        optimizer.zero_grad() # reset gradients
        output = model(data) # determine the outputs of all data points within the batch with the current model
        loss = F.nll_loss(output, target) # calculate the loss corresponding to the data points within the batch
        loss.backward() # calculate the gradients using backpropagation, w.r.t. all parameters in the model
        optimizer.step() # advance the parameters using the gradients.
        if batch_idx % 16 == 0: # print progress
            print('Train Epoch: {} [{}/{} ({:.0f}%)]\tLoss: {:.6f}'.format(
                epoch, batch_idx * len(data), len(train_loader.dataset),
                100. * batch_idx / len(train_loader), loss.item()))

def test(model, test_loader, device = "cpu"):
    test_loss = 0
    correct = 0
    with torch.no_grad(): # no need for gradients
        for data, target in test_loader: # go through all batches within the testing data set
            data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device) # extract image data and target
            output = model(data) # determine the outputs of all data points within the batch with the current model
            test_loss += F.nll_loss(output, target, reduction='sum').item()  # sum up batch loss
            pred = output.argmax(dim=1, keepdim=True)  # get the index of the max log-probability
            correct += pred.eq(target.view_as(pred)).sum().item() # calculate how many predictions are correct

    test_loss /= len(test_loader.dataset) # average the loss

    print('\nTest set: Average loss: {:.4f}, Accuracy: {}/{} ({:.0f}%)\n'.format(
        test_loss, correct, len(test_loader.dataset),
        100. * correct / len(test_loader.dataset)))

    return test_loss, correct / len(test_loader.dataset)

Choosing between procedures and models: validation¶

So far, we have used two data sets: training and testing.

  • The training set was used to calculate the gradients w.r.t. the model parameters and to optimise the model.
  • The test, independent of the training set, was used to evaluate the performance of the model on unseen data. The main purpose of the test set is to assess the real-world performance of the model, therefore it should not be contaminated with the training set.

It is common to use a third data set, called the validation set. There are no set rules, but typically the validation set is a subset of the training set, and it is usually smaller than the training or the test set. The purpose of the validation set is to avoid overfitting: that is, to monitor the performance of the models during optimisation, or to compare models obtained with different hyperparameters (e.g. learning rates, network architecture, etc.)

Here we will use the validation set to calculate the validation loss as well as the percentage of correct assignments on the validation set.

In [24]:
# Update the train() function to calculate the validation loss in every epoch.

def train(model, train_loader, validation_loader, optimizer, epoch, device = "cpu"):
    
    for batch_idx, (data, target) in enumerate(train_loader): # go through all batches within the training data set
        data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device) # extract image data and target
        optimizer.zero_grad() # reset gradients
        output = model(data) # determine the outputs of all data points within the batch with the current model
        loss = F.nll_loss(output, target) # calculate the loss corresponding to the data points within the batch
        loss.backward() # calculate the gradients using backpropagation, w.r.t. all parameters in the model
        optimizer.step() # advance the parameters using the gradients.

    validation_loss = 0
    validation_correct = 0
    with torch.no_grad(): # no need for gradients
        for data, target in validation_loader:
            data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device) # extract image data and target
            output = model(data) # determine the outputs of all data points within the batch with the current model
            validation_loss += F.nll_loss(output, target, reduction='sum').item()  # sum up batch loss
            pred = output.argmax(dim=1, keepdim=True)  # get the index of the max log-probability
            validation_correct += pred.eq(target.view_as(pred)).sum().item() # calculate how many predictions are correct
    return validation_loss, validation_correct / len(validation_loader.dataset)

We take the last 1024 of the original training data points and reserve them as a validation set.

Task¶

Discuss the obtained figure. Explain how our optimisation procedure gives rise to the observed behaviour.

[1 mark]

For the early epochs, the negative log-likelihood is high with low accuracy. This is because the network starts with almost uniform class probabilities. As the number of epochs goes, the model has learned as much as it can within the confinements of the dataset, so the correct fraction plateaus. On the other hand, the loss increases with the number of epochs since the optimiser continues to update the model weights. The negative log-likelihood depends on the probability of the true label. The set of misclassified validation points becomes fixed, thus the confidence in their incorrectness makes the log-probability for true values smaller and thus negative log-likelihood increases.

Hold out method¶

A common practice is to take the best performing model during the optimisation, and use that as the definitive model. You can take a "snapshot" of a model by using the deepcopy() function or save the model to the disk.

In [29]:

Scheduling¶
The observed minimum in the validation loss indicates that after the model performance saturates, subsequent training steps are not particularly useful.


Schedulers try to solve this problem. One of the inputs to the optimiser was the learning rate (lr) parameter, which we set to 1. Schedulers adapt this value according to a recipe, usually decreasing it as the optimisation proceeds. We will use a simple scheduler in the following: every $s$ step the learning rate $\eta$ is updated as $\eta' = \eta \gamma$.


















In [33]:






from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import StepLR





















In [34]:






model = DenseNetwork() # Based on the model definition, we generate an instance of the model, with random weights.
optimizer = optim.Adadelta(model.parameters(), lr=1)

scheduler = StepLR(optimizer, step_size=4, gamma=0.75)

num_epochs = 128

loss = []
correct = []

best_loss = float("inf")
best_correct = 0
best_epoch = 0
best_model = deepcopy(model)

for epoch in tqdm(range(1, 1+num_epochs)):
    val_loss, val_corr = train(model, train_loader, validation_loader, optimizer, epoch)
    scheduler.step()
    
    loss.append(val_loss)
    correct.append(val_corr)
    if val_loss < best_loss:
        best_loss = val_loss       # Update new best loss record
        best_correct = val_corr # Update corresponding accuracy
        best_epoch = epoch                # Record epoch this happened in
        best_model = deepcopy(model)

loss = np.array(loss)
correct = np.array(correct)

The use of a scheduler allows training to take large steps early in the training process, significantly improving accuracy and minimising loss, then taking smaler steps as performance plateaus. Training set size and learning curve¶
So far, another arbitrary setting was the number of training data points we used. Is 1024 too many? Not enough? Using too little leads to a suboptimal model. Using too much requires unnecessary amounts of resources.


It is common practice to train a set of models using increasing number of data points. By looking at some performance metric, such as loss on the validation or test set we can determine an optimal size for the data set, given a model complexity.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)¶
So far, we used a simple, fully connected neural network as our model. We could make it more complex by adding more hidden layers or increasing the number of nodes in the hidden layer(s). Both of these actions would significantly increase the number of parameters, and could potentially require ever larger training sets.


Instead of increasing the number of parameters and the complexity of the model, CNNs aim to extract features which are more geometrically informed than the nodes of hidden layers.


An important ingredient is the convolution operation.

A CNN model¶
Now we're ready to define a CNN model. This one will take a greyscale image (1 channel only!) and


    

  • apply the first convolution layer, this creates 4 new channels
    • 

  • pass the results through a ReLU
    • 

  • apply the second convolution layer, this keeps the 4 channels, but also mixes the previous four
    • 

  • pass the results through a ReLU
    • 

  • apply a max pool
    • 

  • after flattening the result, apply a similar deep neural network as we did before.
    • 



















In [42]:






class CNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(CNN, self).__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 4, 3, 1) # input channels, output channels, size of kernel, stride
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(4, 4, 3, 1)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(576, 16)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(16, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = self.conv2(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = F.max_pool2d(x, 2)
        x = torch.flatten(x,1)
        x = self.fc1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = self.fc2(x)
        output = F.log_softmax(x, dim=1)
        return output

Task¶
Discuss below the differences of the DenseNetwork and CNN models and their respective advantages and disadvantages. Discuss the models you have trained in the broader context of dense and convolutional neural networks, including the state-of-the-art, using literature sources.


[3 mark]






















The DenseNetwork interprets the image as a flat vector, learning patterns from data. In turn, it is more prone to idiosyncratic classifications for unseen data. The key advantage here is that it is fast to develop but requires longer training periods with more data to perform as robustly as a CNN. The CNN model preserves the spatial structure using 2D arrays, yielding higher accuracy however it takes longer to develop as it has varying architectural choices (i.e. kernel sizing, pooling, dense layers). This can take longer to train.


The CNN has been the dominant mode of image recognition in the field of Computer Vision, from biomedical image processing (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2020.04.157) to facial recognition software (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.measen.2023.100800). Its applications are used beyond traditional image detection; time-series data can be converted into images (via Gramian Angular Fields), with CNNs used to predict future data points (https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2504.00378). Whilst state-of-the-art (SOTA) models incorporate attention-based layers (https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2010.11929), large-scale pretraining is required, leaving CNNs as an attractive substitute, with modern CNN performances remaining highly competitive (i.e. ConvNets:
https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2010.11929)


DenseNetworks still serve as the baseline for regressional and classification problems within data science applications. MLP-based vision models offer the performance of SOTA models with competitive inference and pretraining costs (https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2010.11929)

The first neural network model¶
We first build a dense neural network, with a single hidden layer.


This model


    

  1. flattens the $28\times 28$ pixel values into a 1D array, $\mathbf{x}_0$, of $28\times 28 = 784$ numbers;
    2. 

  2. $\mathbf{x}_0$ is transformed into a new vector $\mathbf{x}_1$ of a length of 15, using a parameter matrix $\mathbf{W}_1$ and bias vector $\mathbf{b}_1$: $\mathbf{x}_1 = \mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{x}_0 + \mathbf{b}_1$
    3. 

  3. the elements of $\mathbf{x}_1$ are passed through the rectified linear unit (ReLU) function, obtaining $\mathbf{x}_1'$: $\mathbf{x}_1' = \mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{x}_1)$
    4. 

  4. $\mathbf{x}_1'$ is transformed into a new vector $\mathbf{x}_2$ of a length of 10, using a parameter matrix $\mathbf{W}_2$ and bias vector $\mathbf{b}_2$: $\mathbf{x}_2 = \mathbf{W}_2 \mathbf{x}_1' + \mathbf{b}_2$
    5. 

  5. the elements of $\mathbf{x}_2$ are passed through the $\log \mathrm{softmax}$ function, obtaining $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$
    6. 



$\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$ is the output of the model. We are fitting to 10 categories, therefore we define $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$ as a 10-element vector. The $i$-th element of $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$ corresponds to the log probability of digit $i$, given the input vector $\mathbf{x}_0$.


Below is a visual representation of the neural network. Not all the 784 input features are represented.








































In [57]:






class DenseNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(DenseNetwork, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(784,15) # The first weight matrix and bias vector
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(15,10) # The second weight matrix and bias vector

    def forward(self, x):
        x = torch.flatten(x, 1) # step 1
        x = self.fc1(x) # step 2
        x = F.relu(x) # step 3
        x = self.fc2(x) # step 4
        output = F.log_softmax(x, dim=1) # step 5
        return output

























Activation functions¶
The rectified linear unit (ReLU) function is very popular and it is defined as
$$\textrm{ReLU}(x)=\begin{cases}
x & \textrm{if}\quad x>0\\
0 & \textrm{otherwise}
\end{cases}$$


The $\log \textrm{softmax}$ function operates on a vector input $\mathbf{x}$, resulting in $\mathbf{y}$, where
$$y_i = \log \left( \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j)} \right)
$$

plt.ylabel(r"$y$")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Fitting the model¶
To fit the model we need to define a loss. We will use the negative log likelihood loss function, a common choice in classification tasks.
$$\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{i\in \mathrm{batch}} \tilde{y}_{t_i}(\mathbf{x}_i)$$


where $t_i$ is the target label of the $i$-th data point in the batch, $\tilde{y}_{t_i}$ is the $t_i$-th element of the predicted $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$ vector at data point $\mathbf{x}_i$.
Remember that $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x}_i)$ is the output of the $\log \textrm{softmax}$ function.
The optimiser will minimise this loss function, therefore maximising the predicted log likelihood of the correct label prediction.


In prediction mode, we simply choose the index of the largest predicted log likelihood - this is the category assigned by the model to the datapoint.


















In [65]:






def train(model, train_loader, optimizer, epoch, device = "cpu"):
    
    for batch_idx, (data, target) in enumerate(train_loader): # go through all batches within the training data set
        data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device) # extract image data and target
        optimizer.zero_grad() # reset gradients
        output = model(data) # determine the outputs of all data points within the batch with the current model
        loss = F.nll_loss(output, target) # calculate the loss corresponding to the data points within the batch
        loss.backward() # calculate the gradients using backpropagation, w.r.t. all parameters in the model
        optimizer.step() # advance the parameters using the gradients.
        if batch_idx % 16 == 0: # print progress
            print('Train Epoch: {} [{}/{} ({:.0f}%)]\tLoss: {:.6f}'.format(
                epoch, batch_idx * len(data), len(train_loader.dataset),
                100. * batch_idx / len(train_loader), loss.item()))

def test(model, test_loader, device = "cpu"):
    test_loss = 0
    correct = 0
    with torch.no_grad(): # no need for gradients
        for data, target in test_loader: # go through all batches within the testing data set
            data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device) # extract image data and target
            output = model(data) # determine the outputs of all data points within the batch with the current model
            test_loss += F.nll_loss(output, target, reduction='sum').item()  # sum up batch loss
            pred = output.argmax(dim=1, keepdim=True)  # get the index of the max log-probability
            correct += pred.eq(target.view_as(pred)).sum().item() # calculate how many predictions are correct

    test_loss /= len(test_loader.dataset) # average the loss

    print('\nTest set: Average loss: {:.4f}, Accuracy: {}/{} ({:.0f}%)\n'.format(
        test_loss, correct, len(test_loader.dataset),
        100. * correct / len(test_loader.dataset)))

    return test_loss, correct / len(test_loader.dataset)

Choosing between procedures and models: validation¶
So far, we have used two data sets: training and testing.


    

  • The training set was used to calculate the gradients w.r.t. the model parameters and to optimise the model.
    • 

  • The test, independent of the training set, was used to evaluate the performance of the model on unseen data. The main purpose of the test set is to assess the real-world performance of the model, therefore it should not be contaminated with the training set.
    • 



It is common to use a third data set, called the validation set. There are no set rules, but typically the validation set is a subset of the training set, and it is usually smaller than the training or the test set. The purpose of the validation set is to avoid overfitting: that is, to monitor the performance of the models during optimisation, or to compare models obtained with different hyperparameters (e.g. learning rates, network architecture, etc.)


Here we will use the validation set to calculate the validation loss as well as the percentage of correct assignments on the validation set.


















In [71]:






# Update the train() function to calculate the validation loss in every epoch.

def train(model, train_loader, validation_loader, optimizer, epoch, device = "cpu"):
    
    for batch_idx, (data, target) in enumerate(train_loader): # go through all batches within the training data set
        data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device) # extract image data and target
        optimizer.zero_grad() # reset gradients
        output = model(data) # determine the outputs of all data points within the batch with the current model
        loss = F.nll_loss(output, target) # calculate the loss corresponding to the data points within the batch
        loss.backward() # calculate the gradients using backpropagation, w.r.t. all parameters in the model
        optimizer.step() # advance the parameters using the gradients.

    validation_loss = 0
    validation_correct = 0
    with torch.no_grad(): # no need for gradients
        for data, target in validation_loader:
            data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device) # extract image data and target
            output = model(data) # determine the outputs of all data points within the batch with the current model
            validation_loss += F.nll_loss(output, target, reduction='sum').item()  # sum up batch loss
            pred = output.argmax(dim=1, keepdim=True)  # get the index of the max log-probability
            validation_correct += pred.eq(target.view_as(pred)).sum().item() # calculate how many predictions are correct
    return validation_loss, validation_correct / len(validation_loader.dataset)

Task¶
Discuss the obtained figure. Explain how our optimisation procedure gives rise to the observed behaviour.


[1 mark]






















For the early epochs, the negative log-likelihood is high with low accuracy. This is because the network starts with almost uniform class probabilities. As the number of epochs goes, the model has learned as much as it can within the confinements of the dataset, so the correct fraction plateaus. On the other hand, the loss increases with the number of epochs since the optimiser continues to update the model weights. The negative log-likelihood depends on the probability of the true label. The set of misclassified validation points becomes fixed, thus the confidence in their incorrectness makes the log-probability for true values smaller and thus negative log-likelihood increases.

Scheduling¶
The observed minimum in the validation loss indicates that after the model performance saturates, subsequent training steps are not particularly useful.


Schedulers try to solve this problem. One of the inputs to the optimiser was the learning rate (lr) parameter, which we set to 1. Schedulers adapt this value according to a recipe, usually decreasing it as the optimisation proceeds. We will use a simple scheduler in the following: every $s$ step the learning rate $\eta$ is updated as $\eta' = \eta \gamma$.


















In [80]:






from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import StepLR





















In [81]:






model = DenseNetwork() # Based on the model definition, we generate an instance of the model, with random weights.
optimizer = optim.Adadelta(model.parameters(), lr=1)

scheduler = StepLR(optimizer, step_size=4, gamma=0.75)

num_epochs = 128

loss = []
correct = []

best_loss = float("inf")
best_correct = 0
best_epoch = 0
best_model = deepcopy(model)

for epoch in tqdm(range(1, 1+num_epochs)):
    validation_loss, validation_correct = train(model, train_loader, validation_loader, optimizer, epoch)
    scheduler.step()
    
    loss.append(validation_loss)
    correct.append(validation_correct)
    if validation_loss < best_loss:
        best_loss = validation_loss       # Update new best loss record
        best_correct = validation_correct # Update corresponding accuracy
        best_epoch = epoch                # Record epoch this happened in
        best_model = deepcopy(model)

loss = np.array(loss)
correct = np.array(correct)

ax2.set_ylabel("correct fraction", color="b")
ax2.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="b")

best_idx = best_epoch - 1
ax1.semilogy(best_epoch, loss[best_idx], "ro", markersize=7)
ax2.plot(best_epoch, correct[best_idx], "bo", markersize=7)
ax1.axvline(best_epoch, color="k", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)

plt.show()
















































Task¶
Discuss how the scheduler helped the training process and what the advantages are of using one.


[1 mark]






















The use of a scheduler allows training to take large steps early in the training process, significantly improving accuracy and minimising loss, then taking smaler steps as performance plateaus. This gives a fast and stable method to improve convergence whilst mitigating overfitting.






















Training set size and learning curve¶
So far, another arbitrary setting was the number of training data points we used. Is 1024 too many? Not enough? Using too little leads to a suboptimal model. Using too much requires unnecessary amounts of resources.


It is common practice to train a set of models using increasing number of data points. By looking at some performance metric, such as loss on the validation or test set we can determine an optimal size for the data set, given a model complexity.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)¶
So far, we used a simple, fully connected neural network as our model. We could make it more complex by adding more hidden layers or increasing the number of nodes in the hidden layer(s). Both of these actions would significantly increase the number of parameters, and could potentially require ever larger training sets.


Instead of increasing the number of parameters and the complexity of the model, CNNs aim to extract features which are more geometrically informed than the nodes of hidden layers.


An important ingredient is the convolution operation.






















Exercise¶
In the following code cell you can convince yourself about the operation of the 2D convolution operation. Based on the manually set weights, bias and input, you should be able to work out what the output should be.


Of course, in a practical model weights and biases are set to random initial values and optimisied using data.


















In [ ]:






c1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 1, 3, 1) # input channels, output channels, size of kernel, stride

c1.bias = nn.Parameter(data=torch.tensor([0.5],dtype=torch.float))
weight = torch.tensor(
    [
        [1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
        [0.0, 2.0, 0.0],
        [1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
    ],dtype=torch.float
)
c1.weight = nn.Parameter(data=weight[None,None,:,:])

print(f"weights:\n {weight}")
print(f"bias:\n {c1.bias}")
x = torch.arange(16,dtype=torch.float).reshape((4,4))
x = x[None,None,:,:]
print(f"input:\n{x}")
print(f"output:\n {c1(x)}")

A CNN model¶
Now we're ready to define a CNN model. This one will take a greyscale image (1 channel only!) and


    

  • apply the first convolution layer, this creates 4 new channels
    • 

  • pass the results through a ReLU
    • 

  • apply the second convolution layer, this keeps the 4 channels, but also mixes the previous four
    • 

  • pass the results through a ReLU
    • 

  • apply a max pool
    • 

  • after flattening the result, apply a similar deep neural network as we did before.
    • 



















In [ ]:






class CNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(CNN, self).__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 4, 3, 1) # input channels, output channels, size of kernel, stride
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(4, 4, 3, 1)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(576, 16)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(16, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = self.conv2(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = F.max_pool2d(x, 2)
        x = torch.flatten(x,1)
        x = self.fc1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = self.fc2(x)
        output = F.log_softmax(x, dim=1)
        return output
